questions.q: What does the article mean by a “mistake-plus”?
options: A mistake made twice
Not quite. The article says: A mistake that leads to introspection and so awakens the mind to re-plan better.
A mistake hidden from everyone
Not quite. The article says: A mistake that leads to introspection and so awakens the mind to re-plan better.
A mistake that leads to introspection and so awakens the mind to re-plan better
Yes. Regret alone only disheartens.
A mistake that harms others too
Not quite. The article says: A mistake that leads to introspection and so awakens the mind to re-plan better.
questions.rationale: “A mistake becomes a mistake-plus when it awakens your mind. It thus enables you to re-plan your life.”

questions.q: Which simple formula does the article suggest feeding into one’s thinking in times of difficulty?
options: “It is all but temporary”
Right. No difficulty goes on forever.
“It will always be so”
Not quite. The article says: “It is all but temporary”.
“It could not be helped”
Not quite. The article says: “It is all but temporary”.
“It is someone else’s fault”
Not quite. The article says: “It is all but temporary”.
questions.rationale: “Every difficulty is bound to disappear after some time… So, you have to feed this simple formula into your thinking, ‘It is all but temporary’.”

questions.q: The article calls one principle “a master key to human ethics.” Which?
options: Speak only when spoken to
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
Treat others as you would like them to treat you
Well read. “Like for his brother what he likes for himself.”
Keep to your own people
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
Give more than you receive
Not quite. The article says: Treat others as you would like them to treat you.
questions.rationale: “It is the principle of treating others just as one would like to be treated by them… one single key which suffices to open all locked doors.”

questions.q: How does the article regard a religious act performed for public praise or worldly gain?
options: As a matter between the person and society
Not quite. The article says: As ill-intentioned and without value before God, whatever its outward look.
As better than doing nothing
Not quite. The article says: As ill-intentioned and without value before God, whatever its outward look.
As ill-intentioned and without value before God, whatever its outward look
Correct. God knows the inner reality.
As acceptable if done correctly
Not quite. The article says: As ill-intentioned and without value before God, whatever its outward look.
questions.rationale: “Ostensibly religious acts, if performed for worldly gain or public commendation, are in this sense ill-intentioned.”

questions.q: With whom does the article advise a student to compete?
options: With his brothers and sisters
Not quite. The article says: With his own better self – discovering and developing his particular ability.
With the top scorer in the class
Not quite. The article says: With his own better self – discovering and developing his particular ability.
With students of other schools
Not quite. The article says: With his own better self – discovering and developing his particular ability.
With his own better self – discovering and developing his particular ability
Yes. Not blindly with classmates.
questions.rationale: “Discovering one’s potential and turning it into reality is what is important rather than just blindly competing with others… The competition should be with your own better self.”

questions.q: What should parents chiefly give their children at examination time, according to the article?
options: Rewards for every mark gained
Not quite. The article says: Wise counsel and the principles of life – patience, realism, learning from failure – rather than pressure.
Wise counsel and the principles of life – patience, realism, learning from failure – rather than pressure
Right. Topping exams does not guarantee topping in life.
Constant questioning about their preparation
Not quite. The article says: Wise counsel and the principles of life – patience, realism, learning from failure – rather than pressure.
Comparison with other children
Not quite. The article says: Wise counsel and the principles of life – patience, realism, learning from failure – rather than pressure.
questions.rationale: “They must limit themselves to doing wise counselling. It would be counterproductive if they constantly question their children and apply mental pressure on them to perform.”

questions.q: “Money is a good helper. But it is not a good leader.” What does the article mean?
options: Money should be avoided altogether
Not quite. The article says: Money should serve one’s needs and higher purposes, not become the goal of life.
Money should be given to leaders
Not quite. The article says: Money should serve one’s needs and higher purposes, not become the goal of life.
Wealthy people make poor rulers
Not quite. The article says: Money should serve one’s needs and higher purposes, not become the goal of life.
Money should serve one’s needs and higher purposes, not become the goal of life
Well reasoned. Man is greater than money.
questions.rationale: “Money for the sake of money is bad, but money for the sake of some higher purpose is good; money as a necessity is good, but the money culture per se is a disaster.”

questions.q: How widely did the Prophet define charity?
options: Only what is given to relatives
Not quite. The article says: Every good act – a smile, showing the way, removing a thorn from the road, a kind word.
Every good act – a smile, showing the way, removing a thorn from the road, a kind word
Yes. Not only alms and feeding the poor.
Only gifts made on festivals
Not quite. The article says: Every good act – a smile, showing the way, removing a thorn from the road, a kind word.
Only money given in secret
Not quite. The article says: Every good act – a smile, showing the way, removing a thorn from the road, a kind word.
questions.rationale: “He believed that every good act was a form of charity; smiling at a fellow human being; showing the road to a person who has lost his way; removing hindrances such as thorns and stones from the road…”

questions.q: Asked how the Prophet lived at home, what did Aisha say?
options: He kept apart and was served by others
Not quite. The article says: Like any ordinary man – he swept, mended his sandals, milked the goats and helped the servants.
Like any ordinary man – he swept, mended his sandals, milked the goats and helped the servants
Exactly. Simple living and humility.
He left household matters to servants
Not quite. The article says: Like any ordinary man – he swept, mended his sandals, milked the goats and helped the servants.
He spent the whole day in the mosque
Not quite. The article says: Like any ordinary man – he swept, mended his sandals, milked the goats and helped the servants.
questions.rationale: “‘Like any ordinary man’, she would answer. ‘He would sweep the house, stitch his own clothes, mend his own sandals… help the servants at their work, and eat his meal with them.’”

questions.q: The article says keeping death in mind transforms life. Which change does it mention?
options: One avoids meeting people
Not quite. The article says: One sees how absurd it is to trouble others or feel superior, since one must answer for it.
One loses interest in work
Not quite. The article says: One sees how absurd it is to trouble others or feel superior, since one must answer for it.
One sees how absurd it is to trouble others or feel superior, since one must answer for it
Well read. All we hold is “testing material.”
One gathers more possessions quickly
Not quite. The article says: One sees how absurd it is to trouble others or feel superior, since one must answer for it.
questions.rationale: “It will make you realize… how absurd it is to trouble others, because you will have to answer for this after death… It will make you ashamed of thinking yourself to be superior to others.”
